Title: Material families occupy different stiffness-density regions and require grade-specific screening
Caption: Illustrative nominal stiffness-density points are assigned and do not represent full material-family ranges or sourced design data. CFRP point is longitudinal modulus; transverse properties differ. Temperature and cost entries are qualitative constraints, not maximum-service ratings or current prices. Actual grade, orientation, environment, quality, and manufacturing route must supply the properties for a design decision.

Title: Mechanical material selection screens hard constraints before comparing life and cost
Caption: Conceptual selection workflow rather than a particular material recommendation. Strength and stiffness differ; thermal and chemical environment can change durability. Cost comparisons include manufacturing, inspection, maintenance, and end of life over one common boundary. Verification includes property provenance, geometry, failure modes, manufacturing effects, and appropriate uncertainty or safety factors.

Title: A flat-plate boundary layer grows downstream and can transition from laminar to turbulent flow
Caption: Flat plate with nominal zero pressure gradient. Laminar and turbulent thickness trends are blended across an assigned0.6–0.9 m transition region for illustration, not a solved transitional boundary layer. Surface roughness, disturbances, pressure gradient, and free-stream turbulence affect transition. Boundary-layer edge is a conventional thickness, not a sharp physical interface.

Title: Velocity rises from no slip at the wall to the external stream across the boundary layer
Caption: Assigned laminar flat-plate quartic-profile approximation, U∞10 m/s andν1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Width of each plotted profile is an explanatory scaled velocity, not an actual downstream displacement of the fluid. Height is physical millimeters. The profile satisfies no slip, external velocity, and zero edge gradient; its wall-shear coefficient is approximate rather than exact Blasius.

Title: Separation creates a wake; streamlining can delay separation and reduce pressure drag
Caption: Conceptual two-dimensional flow sketches, not CFD or measured separation angles. Body shape and pressure gradient influence boundary-layer separation; Reynolds number and surface conditions also matter. The streamlined sketch shows a smaller wake in this illustration, not a guaranteed drag value. Friction drag remains, and the upstream/downstream geometry must be compared on a stated reference area.

Title: Drag coefficient varies with Reynolds number and the chosen body shape
Caption: Original assigned log-log trend curves qualitatively follow textbook sphere, long-cylinder, and disk behavior; numerical knots are not digitized experimental data and must not be used for design interpolation. Only the sphere’s low-Re24/Re asymptote is asserted quantitatively. Orientation, aspect ratio, surface roughness, Mach number, and turbulence shift the coefficient and drag-crisis location.

Title: An airfoil pressure difference produces lift; angle of attack changes lift until stall
Caption: Assigned low-speed teaching model, not an actual airfoil polar or CFD result. Pressure difference integrates toCL0.86 at the illustrated6° operating point under the thin-section pressure-lift approximation. The separate CL curve rises linearly to an assigned stall onset12° then declines; real stall depends on geometry, Reynolds number, roughness, and history. Drag vector gives direction only, not a calculated drag coefficient.

Title: Geometric similarity alone does not ensure both Reynolds and Froude similarity
Caption: Assigned quarter-scale model, identical fluid kinematic viscosity and gravity, prototype speed2 m/s. The diagram lengths are schematic rather than exact scale drawings. Choose the dominant physical similarity or change fluid/conditions; matching one number does not guarantee matching another. Compressibility may also require Mach matching; boundaries, roughness, and force scaling must be checked separately.

Title: Affinity laws relate corresponding pump points at geometrically similar operating conditions
Caption: Assigned pump head curve H1=40−.002Q1² and constant-density, same-diameter speed change. Scaled curves use Q2=sQ1 and H2=s²H1; power ratio assumes comparable efficiency. Dots are corresponding similarity points, not operating points against a specified system curve. Fan pressure uses analogous speed trends at fixed density; changing density, cavitation, compressibility, or efficiency can require corrections.

Title: A moving disturbance outruns acoustic waves when its Mach number exceeds one
Caption: Source moves right through a stationary uniform medium with sound speed a; at the shown instant the source is at the origin and earlier wave centers lie behind it. These are small-disturbance Mach cones, not finite-strength shock angles. Hypersonic convention is roughly M≥5; thermal/chemical effects are not modeled. Panel coordinate spans differ to fit the emission histories.

Title: Isentropic deceleration converts kinetic energy into stagnation enthalpy
Caption: Ideal air, γ=1.4 and R=287 J/(kg·K); reversible adiabatic stagnation. Static and total states are distinct. A real probe or shock can lose total pressure; the drawn local streamline is conceptual. Stagnation temperature follows the steady-flow energy balance.

Title: A sonic throat connects subsonic inlet flow to a supersonic nozzle branch
Caption: Quasi-one-dimensional ideal-gas nozzle with A/At=1+4(x−0.5)². Choked design branch is shock-free; the unchoked branch has A*/At=1/1.2. Area alone admits two Mach roots; reservoir and back pressure select the realized solution. Relative radius is √(A/At).

Title: A converging nozzle reaches a mass-flow plateau once the throat chokes
Caption: Steady converging nozzle, ideal air, discharge coefficient1. Above the critical ratio the exit is subsonic; below it the throat is sonic and reducing back pressure does not raise mass flow. This threshold is for a converging nozzle, not every converging-diverging nozzle back-pressure regime.

Title: A normal shock raises static pressure and temperature while lowering total pressure
Caption: Ideal air normal shock, no heat/work transfer. Conservation of mass, momentum, and total enthalpy gives the stated downstream values. Entropy rises; total pressure is not conserved. Static temperature rises even though total temperature remains540 K.

Title: Back pressure selects nozzle flow and the external expansion or compression
Caption: Same ideal nozzle geometry as1301. Internal normal-shock branch is calculated with downstream A* adjusted for total-pressure loss. Dashed external lines are assigned ambient levels, not resolved jet pressure profiles; both moderate off-design cases retain the plotted shock-free internal branch. Boundary- layer separation is excluded.

Title: Choose gas-flow models using Mach number, density variation, and process physics
Caption: Model-selection decision tree. M≈0.3 is a common screening scale, not a universal accuracy guarantee. Strong heating, large pressure changes, or long ducts can require density variation at low local Mach number. The two branches identify an approximation choice; assumptions must fit the particular process.

Title: Balance fuel atoms before adding excess air and nitrogen to the products
Caption: Assigned methane fuel and simplified dry air:1 mol O2 per3.76 mol N2. Product water is included in wet products. Fuel sulfur, argon, humidity, CO, and dissociation are excluded. Atom balance precedes any energy calculation.

Title: Twenty percent excess air leaves oxygen in the complete-combustion products
Caption: One-kmol methane basis, complete combustion with20% excess simplified dry air. Theoretical O2 requirement is2 kmol; actual is2.4. Dry products exclude water:1 CO2+0.4 O2+9.024 N2. Unburned species and dissociation are excluded.

Title: Dry flue-gas fractions renormalize the mixture after water is removed
Caption: Same complete methane reaction with20% excess air as1307. Gas composition is on a mole basis. Dry sampling changes the denominator rather than creating or removing fuel atoms; condensed water must remain in the overall material balance.

Title: Fuel heating value and sensible enthalpy balance product enthalpy and heat loss
Caption: One-kmol methane energy basis at reference298 K; assigned LHV802 MJ/kmol with product water vapor. All sensible enthalpies use the same reference. HHV instead assumes liquid product water at the reference and requires consistent phase accounting. Arrow widths are qualitative.

Title: Adiabatic flame temperature is the product temperature that closes the energy balance
Caption: Teaching energy model with assigned constant species heat capacities: CO2 .040, H2O .035, N2 .032 MJ/(kmol·K). No losses, no dissociation, negligible kinetic energy. The estimate is not a high-temperature equilibrium prediction; real cp(T), dissociation, fuel composition, and air preheat alter Tad.

Title: Combustion quality depends on air ratio as well as mixing, residence time, and temperature
Caption: Qualitative schematic, arbitrary relative scales. Rich mixtures can leave incomplete products; excess air can increase stack losses. Lean operation can still form CO if the flame cools or mixing is poor. Curves are not measured emissions, combustion limits, or a calibrated efficiency model.

Title: Combustion calculations link material balance to energy and operating constraints
Caption: Conceptual calculation sequence. Product composition assumptions must match available oxygen and reaction completeness. Energy closure does not demonstrate emissions compliance or safe operation; fuel handling, ventilation, flame stability, and equipment-specific protective functions belong to the actual system evaluation.

Title: A psychrometric state is located by dry-bulb temperature and humidity ratio
Caption: Original SI chart using ASHRAE liquid-water saturation equations; h is referenced to0°C dry air and liquid water. Dashed lines are enthalpy; dotted lines are10,20,25°C thermodynamic wet bulb. State A is assigned; chart is a teaching view at standard atmospheric pressure.

Title: Sensible heating and cooling move horizontally when no moisture is added or removed
Caption: Assigned constant humidity ratio path15→35°C. The upper leftward arrow identifies cooling and is offset only for legibility. Path must stay above the dew point; below it condensation changes W and sensible-only treatment fails.

Title: A wet cooling coil removes sensible heat and condenses water vapor
Caption: Assigned inlet30°C50% RH and ideal saturated outlet12°C,1 kg/s dry air. Straight path is a schematic connection between endpoints; a real coil path depends on bypass factor and surface condition. Exact cooling balance includes outgoing condensate liquid enthalpy: Qout=ṁda(hA−hB)−ṁcond hliquid,B.

Title: Direct evaporative cooling reduces dry bulb while increasing humidity ratio
Caption: Assigned35°C30% RH inlet cooled to22°C on a thermodynamic wet-bulb line. Water is supplied at that wet-bulb temperature, giving exact adiabatic energy balance under the chart equations. Evaporation increases W without condensation. Saturation is not assumed at the outlet.

Title: Adiabatic air mixing balances dry-air mass, water vapor, and enthalpy
Caption: Assigned outdoor35°C50% RH and return24°C50% RH at the same pressure. Mixed state follows exact W and h mass weighting; the chart connector is nearly straight because moist-air cp depends on W. Mass weights are dry-air rates, not total moist-air rates. No condensation occurs.

Title: Building cooling loads include sensible and latent contributions
Caption: Conceptual load decomposition. Envelope conduction and most equipment loads are predominantly sensible; people and outdoor moisture can add latent loads. Ventilation is intentional outdoor air; infiltration is uncontrolled leakage. Solar gain, schedules, humidity, and dynamic storage require stated design conditions and methods.

Title: Refrigerators and heat pumps use the same cycle with different useful heat outputs
Caption: Assigned steady refrigeration cycle, positive magnitudes: QH=QL+Win. Compressor work enters, evaporator heat enters from the cold load, condenser heat exits to the hot load. Expansion valve is approximately isenthalpic. COP is dimensionless and can exceed1; values are assigned, not rated performance.

Title: A helical compression spring loads its wire primarily in torsional shear
Caption: Assigned compression spring D30 mm,d3 mm. Wahl factor combines curvature and direct shear. The wire section is enlarged separately, not to coil scale. Hookean spring behavior does not by itself guarantee stress acceptability or fatigue life; material and cycle information are required.

Title: Spring rate relates force and deflection before contact or instability
Caption: Same D30 mm,d3 mm spring as1320,8 active coils and assigned free length75 mm. Solid height depends on end style; the selected closed-ground spring has Nt10 and Ls30 mm. Diagram plots only the assigned linear range, not the coil-contact response.

Title: Series springs carry the same force; parallel springs undergo the same deflection
Caption: Assigned spring rates10 and20 N/mm; rigid massless attachments and linear axial deformation. In series, δtotal=δ1+δ2; in parallel, Ftotal=F1+F2. No preload, damping, contact, or geometric stiffness effects are included.
